identity.title: RGB Mood Light
identity.tagline: One data wire, unlimited full-color LEDs — the addressable-LED trick behind every RGB strip.

goal: Drive a strip of WS2812B ("NeoPixel") addressable LEDs from a single Arduino pin, smoothly cycling through colors — and understand why this is fundamentally different from wiring up three separate red/green/blue LEDs.
simpleSummary: Make a strip of full-color LEDs smoothly cycle through colors.
howItWorks: A normal LED needs one wire per LED (plus shared ground). A WS2812B strip sidesteps that entirely: each tiny LED actually contains its own microchip that reads a precise, timed data signal on a single wire, keeps the color instructions meant for it, and passes the rest down the line to the next LED — like a bucket brigade. This is why you can control 1 LED or 500 LEDs from the exact same single Arduino pin: the wiring never changes, only the software's LED count does. The Adafruit_NeoPixel library handles the extremely precise, microsecond-level timing this protocol requires — timing so tight it can't realistically be hand-written with digitalWrite() calls.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
The Adafruit NeoPixel library, installed via the Arduino IDE Library Manager

components.note: a short strip (a handful of LEDs) is enough

circuitDiagramCaption: Only three wires total: DIN (data), 5V, and GND — the same three pins regardless of how many LEDs are on the strip.

wiringSteps.instruction: Identify the strip's DIN (data in) end — WS2812B strips are directional and usually have an arrow silkscreened showing signal flow.
wiringSteps.detail: Connecting to the DOUT end instead simply won't work — the strip's chips only listen for data flowing in the printed direction.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the strip's DIN to Arduino D6.
wiringSteps.detail: Any digital pin works here — unlike PWM fading, this project doesn't need a ~ (PWM) pin, since the library generates its own precise timing in software.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the strip's 5V to Arduino 5V, and GND to Arduino GND.
wiringSteps.detail: For a short strip (under ~8 LEDs) powering directly from the Arduino's 5V pin is fine; a longer strip can draw more current than the Arduino can safely supply and needs its own 5V power source.

wiringSteps.instruction: Install the Adafruit NeoPixel library (Tools > Manage Libraries in the Arduino IDE) before uploading the code.
wiringSteps.detail: This is a software step, not a wiring one, but it's the step most likely to trip up a first-timer — the code won't compile without it.

code.explanation: setPixelColor() only updates a color value in the Arduino's memory — it doesn't touch the physical strip at all. show() is the line that actually sends the whole buffer of colors down the data wire in one precisely-timed burst, which is why it's easy to forget and wonder why nothing changed. setAllPixels() is a small helper that sets every LED to the same color and then calls show() once, rather than repeating that pattern for each color change.

expectedBehavior: The entire strip lights up as one solid color, cycling through red, green, blue, and warm amber, holding each for one second.

troubleshooting.fix: Confirm you're wired to the DIN end, not DOUT, and double-check NUM_LEDS matches your strip's actual LED count.

troubleshooting.issue: Colors look wrong (e.g. red shows as green).
troubleshooting.fix: Change NEO_GRB to NEO_RGB in the strip constructor — different WS2812B batches use different internal color orderings.

troubleshooting.issue: Only some of the LEDs respond.
troubleshooting.fix: Check for a physical break or bad solder joint partway down the strip — since each LED passes data to the next, one bad connection cuts off everything after it.
This is almost always a power problem on longer strips — add a dedicated 5V supply and a large (~1000µF) capacitor across its output, and keep the Arduino and strip grounds connected.

extensions: Animate a single colored pixel chasing down the strip instead of lighting everything the same color.
Add a photoresistor (LDR) so the strip only lights up once it's dark (combine with Light-Activated Night Lamp).
Map a potentiometer or joystick axis to hue for a manually-tunable mood light.
Drive the strip's colors from a rotary encoder's position instead of a fixed color sequence.
